Sākamedha
------------------------------------------
An आहिताग्नि (one who has ceremonially established the Vedic fires) was expected to perform a particular group of sacrifices—known as Cāturmāsya—once every four months. (See CĀTURMĀSYA.) Each of them was called a parvan (part or joint). The third of these is साकमेध.
These sacrifices marked the advent of a particular season.
The साकमेध was to be performed at the beginning of the hemanta-ṛtu (autumn), on the full-मोओन् day of the month of Kārttika or Mārgaśīrṣa (November). The sacrifice is of the इष्टि type (See IṢṬI for details.) and is spread over two days.
On the preliminary day, three iṣṭis are performed to the three deities: अग्नि-anīkavat, सान्तपन-Maruts and gṛha-medhin-Maruts. The offerings to these, respectively, are: a cake on eight potsherds, a चरु (porridge from unpounded rice or barley grains) and another चरु boiled in milk of all the cows belonging to the sacrificer.
The priests and the sons as also grandsons of the sacrificer are to partake of the remainings of these offerings.
On the principal day, a होम is performed with a darvī (wooden spoon), scraping out the remainder of the cooked rice of the previous day.
An interesting (and intriguing?) part of the rite is to bring a bull and make it bellow! It is later on gifted away.
This is then followed by a महाहविस् (great offerings) and Mahāpitṛ-यज्ञ dedicated to certain classes of पितृस् (manes) like barhiṣadpitṛs and agniṣvātta-पितृस्.

śākta
(‘worshipper of शक्ति [or Divine मोथेर्]’)
------------------------------------------
Worshippers of God, in हिन्दुइस्म्, are generally divided into three groups: the vaiṣṇavas, the śaivas and the śāktas. विष्णु, शिव and शक्ति (Divine मोथेर्, पार्वती and her aspects) are, respectively, the deities they worship. Of course, even these deities are facets of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
The religion and the philosophy of the Śāktas is contained in the तन्त्रस्.
See also TANTRAS.

Śāktāgamas
------------------------------------------
Āgamas are a special class of Hindu religious literature devoted to the propagation of the various sects centred round the cult-deities. They are generally classified into three groups viz., शैवागमस्, शाक्तागमस् and Vaiṣṇavāgamas, dealing with the three deities शिव, शक्ति (or the Divine मोथेर्, usually an aspect of पार्वती) and विष्णु.
The शाक्तागमस् are also called तन्त्रस्. See TANTRAS for details.

Śaktipīṭhas
(‘Seats of मोथेर् (cult)’ )
------------------------------------------
See under TANTRAS.

Sāketa
------------------------------------------
Sāketa is another name for अयोध्या, the capital of the country कोसल.
It is rather intriguing that this name for अयोध्या is not found in the Rāmāyaṇa of वाल्मीकि, though it has been mentioned in the Raghuvaṁśa (5.31) of कालिदास (200 B. C.). By the time of गौतम बुद्ध (6th century B. C.) it was considered one of the six great cities of Bharatavarṣa. In all the works of Buddhists, Jains, Greeks and of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.), अयोध्या has always been referred to as साकेत only.

śakticālanī-mudrā
(‘pose of the body that helps in activating the Kuṇḍalini’)
------------------------------------------
Śakti is the कुण्डलिनी power, the basic and total energy of every human being, imagined to be like a coiled serpent, lying at the root of the spinal column. The yogic exercise that helps this power to be roused and move towards the सहस्रार-चक्र in the head is called ‘śakticālanī-मुद्रा’. Some of the steps involved in its practice are: sitting with a loin cloth only, smearing the body with holy ash (vibhūti), siddhāsana posture, special प्राणायाम techniques as instructed by the गुरु and so on.
Being a complicated exercise, it has to be practised directly under the guidance of an expert teacher of योग.
See also CAKRAS.

śakuna
(‘omen,’ ‘prognostic sign’)
------------------------------------------
Belief in the supernatural is a common trait of humanity all over the world, even from the most ancient times.
Śakuna means a bird in general. Even in the Ṛgveda (10.16

), the bird kapota (pigeon) has been regarded as a harbinger of impending evil and misfortune. Hence the word शकुन gradually came to mean premonition of evil conveyed by the cries, the sounds and the movements of birds and of other animals. This, gradually, developed into a science of prognostication.
There is a vast literature on this subject. Some of the works are: Matsya-purāṇa (Chapters 237, 241 and 243); Agnipurāṇa (Chapters 230 to 232) Padma-purāṇa (4.100.65 to 126); Bṛhatsaṁhitā (Chapters 85 to 95); Bṛhadyogayātrā (Chapters 23 to 27) and Vasantarāja-śakuna.
The last is a comprehensive work belonging to the early part of the eighth century and has been quoted extensively by later writers on this subject.
The details given in these works regarding the śakunas and their interpretations are, to say the least, मिन्द्-boggling!
The following is a short consolidated list of birds, animals and other living beings whose sounds and movements are considered as śakunas, good or bad: crow, eagle, owl, cat, snake, chameleon, lizard, dog, jackal and frog as also human beings.
The prognostication differs from animal to animal and from case to case. In the case of crows and cats, it is their movement across our path that indicates the results. In the case of dogs, jackals and lizards it is their sound. In some cases, it may be the very sight of a person or an object.
Results indicated may relate to travelling, success or otherwise of an important work, diseases and their cure, wealth and poverty, promotion or demotion in service, harmony or disharmony in the family, good rains or drought, welfare or danger to the country and so on.
Some other omens like the throbbing of one’s limbs or sneezing are also included in the list of śakunas.
A sample of the śakunas may now be given just to give an idea of the subject:
When a person has started on a journey and sees a cat moving across his path from left to the right, it is a bad sign. If he sees married ladies carrying water pots or milk, or, an elephant or a horse, it is a good omen.
When a person is thinking about some important work, and someone sneezes once in his presence, it indicates failure of that work. Similarly, if he finds that his right limbs are throbbing, it indicates success. (For women, throbbing of the left limbs is considered auspicious.)
By sincere prayer to God, the evil effects prognosticated may be eliminated or minimised.

Śakuntalā
------------------------------------------
The origins of the well-known legend of शकुन्तला based on which the great poet कालिदास (2nd century B. C.) wrote his immortal drama Abhijñāna-śākuntalam lie in the Mahābhārata (Ādiparva, Chapters 68-74) as also the Padmapurāṇa (Svarga-khaṇḍa).
She was born to Menakā (a nymph) from विश्वामित्र, to wreck whose austerities इन्द्र, the king of the gods, had sent her. However, as both the parents abandoned her, the śakunta birds (ravens) took care of her, thereby getting her the name शकुन्तला.
The sage कण्व who found the abandoned baby, carried her to his own hermitage and brought her up as his foster daughter.
When she had grown into a beautiful young woman, दुष्यन्त, the king of the lunar race happened to visit कण्व’s hermitage. They fell in love with each other and married according to the गान्धर्व rites. (See VIVĀHA for details.) The same was approved by the sage कण्व who came to know about it later.
In course of time शकुन्तला gave birth to a heroic child whose strength and valour astonished everyone. He was named Sarvadamana as also भरत.
Later, when शकुन्तला went with भरत and the disciples of the sage कण्व to दुष्यन्त to live with him, he hesitated to accept her. At the intervention of an ākāśavāṇi (a celestial message from an unseen god), he accepted her as his queen and coronated भरत as the crown-prince. The name भारतवर्ष or Bhārata for India and the lineage of Bharatavaṁśa started from him.
There is a slight deviation in the story as given by कालिदास. Due to a curse of the sage Durvāsa who was once ignored by शकुन्तला, दुष्यन्त could not recognise her. However, when the signet ring he had given to her was accidentally lost but miraculously recovered and shown to him, he remembered everything and gracefully accepted her.

sākṣī
(‘witness’)
------------------------------------------
A sākṣin or साक्षी is one who witnesses the happenings around him in a detached way, and can give an unbiased account.
In the Hindu judicial system a साक्षी or a witness is accepted as reliable if he comes from a respectable family, is deeply religious by temperament, is devoted to truth and is straightforward.
A few of the interesting descriptions of an unreliable witness are: shifting the position constantly, licking the corner of his own lips, sweat on the forehead, change of colour of the face, faltering speech and contradictory statements.
In Vedānta, the jīvātman (the individual Self) is called साक्षी or साक्षी-चैतन्य since he is a witness to all the three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, viz., जाग्रत् (waking), स्वप्न (dreaming) and सुषुप्ति (deep sleep).
Ātman or ब्रह्मन् also is called साक्षी in the उपनिषद्स् (vide Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.11) and the Bhagavadgītā (9.18) since he is witnessing everything, but is unaffected by the changes of the empirical world.

Śakuni
------------------------------------------
Śakuni of the Mahābhārata could rival even Satan in his villainy and craftiness. If दुर्योधन’s heart was full of the raging fire of jealousy and hatred, शकुनि was the breezy wind that spread it in his whole personality, ultimately destroying his entire race.
He was the eldest son of the king Subala of the country of गान्धार. गान्धारी, the chief queen of the blind king धृतराष्ट्र, was his sister. Ever since her मर्रिअगे, शकुनि started living in हस्तिनापुर, the capital of the kings of the कुरु race.
He had the master-मिन्द् of an evil genius and relentlessly prodded Duryo-dhana in his wicked pursuits.
His nefarious designs and vile deeds may briefly be listed as follows: cheating the Pāṇḍavas in the game of dice; advising दुर्योधन to decimate the Pāṇḍavas by any and every means; encouraging दुर्योधन to exhibit his glory, wealth and power before the Pāṇḍavas living as recluses in the forest and so on. He too participated in the कुरुक्षेत्र war and was killed by सहदेव on the last day.
He is said to have been born out of the anger of the देवस् or gods, to destroy righteousness (Ādiparva 63.111).
See also MAHĀBHĀRATA.
The epics and the पुराणस् mention a few other Śakunis like a serpent, a demon, a king and a sage.

Śākambharī
(‘One who is full of vegetables’)
------------------------------------------
In the Durgāsaptaśatī (11.49) the Divine मोथेर्, while addressing the gods who had supplicated her, tells them that when severe drought affects the world, she will bring out plenty of śāka or nourishing vegetables out of herself and save the famished people.
She is an aspect of दुर्गा having sixteen hands, carrying in them the following items: spear, noose, skull-cup, bow, arrow, thunderbolt, goad, shield, conch, discus, mace, snake, sword, magic wand and cudgel. One hand shows the abhayamudrā (gesture of protection).
She is described as the मोथेर् of the three worlds Trailokyajananī.
The Mahābhārata (Vanaparva 84.13) describes a place of पिल्ग्रिमगे known as शाकम्भरी. ड़स्तिन्ग् at this place improves one’s health.

Śakti
(‘[Divine] Power [as Goddess]’)
------------------------------------------
The universe that we see and experience is a bundle of energy, both packed and unpacked. This is the discovery of modern science, which incidentally, has demolished the distinction between matter and energy. According to it, there is one basic energy behind all forms of matter and energy. However, it seems to be still far off from discovering the relationship between matter on the one hand, and, मिन्द् and life on the other. Are they also, though apparently poles apart, manifestations of the same basic energy? Could it be that the same energy or matter, at one level of vibration, is called ‘matter’, at another, ‘mind’ and yet another, ‘life’? Modern science or the modern scientists, devoting most of their attention to the manifest material universe may not even be prepared to concede this possibility! Hindu philosophy, based on the Vedānta and a group of works based on the Vedānta and more commonly known as the तन्त्रस् मोथेर्.">1 postulates exactly this! The source and sustenance of all च्रेअतिओन्, whether at the level of matter or life or मिन्द्, is one and one only. It is शक्ति (= energy). ब्रह्मन् (the Absolute) of the Vedānta and शक्ति or देवी of the तन्त्रस् are identical. When that ‘energy’ is in a static condition, with neither evolution nor involution, when the universe to be created is not even in a seed-form as it were, it is called ब्रह्मन्. When it starts evolving into this च्रेअतिओन्, sustains it and withdraws it back into itself, it is called शक्ति. If ब्रह्मन् is the coiled serpent in sleep, शक्ति is the same serpent in motion. If ब्रह्मन् is likened to the word, शक्ति is its meaning. If ब्रह्मन् is like fire, शक्ति is its burning power. The two are inseparable: one in two and two in one.
In the Hindu mythological literature, as also in the तन्त्रस्, this energy is always pictured as a female deity, the देवी, as the consort of its counterpart male deity. Each member of the Trinity has his शक्ति or देवी as his consort: सरस्वती of ब्रह्मा, लक्ष्मी of विष्णु and पार्वती of शिव. However, the मोथेर्-cult that has evolved over the last few centuries is predominantly centered round पार्वती, the consort of शिव.
Mother-worship and मोथेर्-cult are not alien to the Vedic religion as some suggest. The concept of Aditi—the मोथेर् of gods, personification of nature, and the Ambhṛṇīsūkta as also the Rātrīsūkta of the Ṛgveda clearly contain the origins of मोथेर्-worship
See also LAKṢMĪ, PĀRVATĪ, and SARASVATĪ.

Śākalya
------------------------------------------
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (3.9) describes in detail, the philosophical dispu-tation between याज्ञवल्क्य and Vidagdha शाकल्य in the court of the king जनक-Vaideha. The discussion centered round the number of देवस् or gods. Ultimately, याज्ञवल्क्य won and शाकल्य lost his life due to the curse of the former. The main reason was that शाकल्य was ‘Vidagdha’, vain and arrogant due to his scholarship.
Some say that Vidagdha was his name (since he was a great scholar) whereas the word शाकल्य indicated that he was the son of the sage Śakala.
The Nirukta (6.28) mentions one शाकल्य as a padapāṭhakāra (an expert in breaking the words of the Vedic Saṁhitā—See GHANAPĀṬHA.) of the Ṛgveda.
Another शाकल्य is mentioned by पाणिनि (circa 500 B. C.) four times in his Aṣṭādhyāyī. He was probably a grammarian.
The well-known sage कश्यप was once saved from public ridicule by a teacher, शाकल्य by name, who prescribed some special purificatory rites.

Śākinī
------------------------------------------
She is an aspect of the Divine मोथेर् (Śakti or पार्वती).
Each of the six चक्रस् or psychic centres in the human body (See CAKRAS.) is associated with a शक्ति as the presiding deity. The शक्ति of the विशुद्धचक्र is called शाकिनी, the शिव aspect being सदाशिव.
She wears yellow garments and has four hands in which she carries bow, arrow, noose and goad.
